Hi Sergio —

Thanks for the proposal last week. A couple of procurement questions came up when we ran the numbers:

- How do you round token usage per call? Our engineering team generates very long single-turn queries (up to ~50k tokens) when we fetch full product histories. Do you round up to a quantum per call or per N tokens?
- Does prefix/KV caching reduce billable tokens on the invoice (i.e., do cached token matches count as 0 or do you credit some percentage)?
- If we stream assistant output vs full-response, is there any different treatment for the minimums/quantum?

Could you send a short sample pre-invoice for a 10M token-month scenario with ~20% cache-hit and 5% streaming overhead so we can show leadership? Also please point us to the SOW / DocuSign when ready.

From: Sergio Alvarez <sergio.alvarez@redwood.com>

Hi Elena —

Thanks for the clear list. Short answers first, then a worked example.

1) Rounding / quantum:
- For hosted API calls we bill tokens consumed and apply a per-request quantum of 25 tokens (i.e., usage rounded up to the nearest 25).
- For streaming calls we apply the same 25-token quantum per stream-chunk; for very long single-turn requests we also amortize long-context retrieval across the request but still apply the quantum on the final billed count.

2) Prefix/KV caching credits:
- Cache hits are credited as "cache-hit tokens" and reduce billable tokens. By default we cap credits to 30% of committed monthly tokens for Dedicated commitments; over that, cache hits simply reduce the billed usage but do not convert to negative invoices. For hosted (pay-as-you-go) customers there is no cap — actual hits reduce billed tokens directly.

3) Streaming vs non-streaming:
- No special premium for streaming in unit price, but you will see slightly higher token counts due to chunking overhead; we model a ~3–7% overhead depending on chunk size.

Worked example (10,000,000 monthly quota, 20% cache-hit, 5% streaming overhead):
- Gross token consumption (application telemetry): 10,000,000 tokens
- Estimated streaming overhead: +5% -> 10,500,000 tokens
- Cache-hit reduction (20% of gross): -2,100,000 tokens
- Net billable tokens: 8,400,000 tokens
- Apply 25-token quantum rounding: round up to nearest 25 -> 8,400,000 is already divisible; final billed tokens = 8,400,000

If instead a subset of calls are single-turn 50k-token requests we still round per-call to nearest 25 — so seven 50k calls would be billed as 350,000 tokens (plus quantum adjustments per call if needed).

I've attached a small workbook with three sample scenarios (orchard_pricing_examples.xlsx) and the updated pricing sheet (pricing_sheet_v2.pdf).

Next steps: I can drop a sample pre-invoice (pdf) showing line items and credits and share a DocuSign SOW link once procurement confirms the commit scale.

Regards,

Hi Elena — looping in the Dedicated commit specifics.

- Spike months with very high cache-hit percentage: the accounting flow is: gross usage -> apply cache-hit credits (up to cap) -> committed allowance applied -> any remaining usage charged as overage at committed rate.
  * Example: gross 25,000,000; cache hits 12,000,000 (48%) -> cache-credit applied = min(12,000,000, 30% * commit). If commit=10,000,000 tokens then cap = 3,000,000 credit. So credit = 3,000,000; remaining cache hits beyond cap simply reduce consumption but not via additional credit.

- On split calls: yes, each API call is evaluated independently for quantum rounding. For high-frequency split architectures you will see quantum amplification; we can mitigate by using a bulk "batching" route or by increasing request payloads where feasible. We can model that tradeoff in your workbook.

I'll attach a short note explaining caching-credit order and an example pre-invoice we typically produce for procurement.

— Vanessa Ortiz
